name: Concept Art and World-Building
title: Concept Art and World-Building
answer: Concept art and world-building cover the visual and narrative development that happens before a film, game, or series is produced. The work includes character design, environment and prop design, mood and colour studies, and the visual rules that make a fictional place feel consistent. It sits between illustration and production design, and it serves directors, writers, and art departments who need to see an idea before committing money to it. Generative tools now sit alongside sketchbooks and 3D blockouts in this stage, used for ideation rather than as a replacement for the artist's judgement.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A concept artist typically works on a tablet with software such as Photoshop, Procreate, or Blender, and increasingly with generative image models accessed through a browser or a local install. Studios run these models on cloud GPUs or on workstations with a capable graphics card, and many keep a shared library of prompts, style references, and trained checkpoints so a team can reproduce a look. Asset management matters as much as the model itself, because a production needs to find the approved version of a design months later. Pipeline tools like ShotGrid or Perforce often hold the approved art alongside the rest of the production data.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually starts with a brief, then moves through thumbnails, roughs, and refined paintings, with review rounds at each stage. Artists use generative models to explore silhouettes, lighting, and material ideas quickly, then paint over or repaint the results to fix anatomy, perspective, and design logic. Reference gathering, photobashing, and 3D blockouts remain common, and a final piece is often a composite of several passes. The artist's job is to make choices, not to accept the first output, and the approved design has to be clear enough for a modeller or costumer to build from.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership and provenance are live issues because generative outputs may draw on training data whose rights are contested, and studios vary in whether they allow such tools on a project. Contracts often require artists to disclose tool use, and some productions ban generative images from final assets while permitting them in early exploration. Style imitation raises its own concerns, particularly where a living artist's work is named in a prompt or used to train a model. Keeping prompt records, model versions, and source references helps a studio show where a design came from if a claim is later made.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration between generative tools and the existing 3D and painting pipeline, with more control over pose, camera, and lighting rather than pure text prompts. Studios are also building internal libraries of approved styles and characters so that generated work stays on model. The role of the concept artist is shifting toward direction and curation, with less time spent on repetitive rendering and more on design decisions. How rights and credit are handled will shape which tools studios adopt and how artists are paid for work that a model helped produce.
